exercise1.prompt: person with name Alice, age 25 and city Boston; print the name and the age

hiddenCases.name: the name and the age are printed

exercise1.hint: A dictionary is written with curly braces and a colon between each key and its value. You reach a value by naming its key in square brackets, not by counting positions.

exercise2.prompt: car with brand Toyota and model Camry; add year 2020, change model to Corolla, print it

cases.name: car ends up with brand, model and year

hiddenCases.name: the model was changed, not added alongside
car has three keys, not four

exercise2.hint: Assigning to a key is both how you add one and how you replace one, and Python cannot tell you which you meant. Keys are case-sensitive, so "Model" and "model" are two different keys.

questions.prompt: What does person["height"] do when person has no "height" key?
choices: Adds the key with the value None
questions.explain: Reading a missing key is an error, not a blank. person.get("height") is the version that hands back None instead.

questions.prompt: car["year"] = 2020 on a dictionary that has no "year" key does what?
choices: Adds the key with that value
questions.explain: Assignment adds the key if it is missing and overwrites it if it is not. That is convenient, and it is also why a typo in a key name silently creates a second entry.

questions.prompt: Which of these can be used as a dictionary key?
questions.explain: A key has to be immutable, so a list cannot be one. A tuple can, which is one of the quiet reasons tuples exist.

questions.prompt: Given person = {"name": "Alice"}, you print the name with print(person[___]).
questions.explain: The key goes inside the brackets, quoted, because it is a string. Without quotes Python looks for a variable called name instead.
